1.text: Module docstring: this lab implements Byte-Pair Encoding from scratch, then compares character-level and BPE tokenization with a simple bigram model.

20.text: This lab is mostly about counting and merging, but we still need a little math later to measure whether the learned subwords actually help the language model.

21.text: BPE learns entirely from the corpus itself, so the first step is simply to find the raw names file we will mine for repeated character patterns.

22.text: The merge history depends on corpus statistics, so we keep the setup stable enough that the same subwords emerge from run to run.

24.text: BPE is a cumulative greedy process: early merges shape every later token, so reproducibility matters more than it first appears.

29.text: Locate the shared names corpus. Every later merge rule will be discovered from these strings alone, with no hand-written vocabulary.

33.text: A tiny but realistic corpus: enough repeated fragments for subwords like an, er, and ia to emerge naturally.

34.text: Fetch the file from the internet once and save it locally. After this first download, every future run loads instantly from disk.

43.text: Every unique character gets an integer id. BOS marks the start and end of each sequence — the model learns when to stop generating.

44.text: Collect every unique character (a-z), this becomes the base vocabulary, same as lab 01.

45.text: Character-to-integer mapping. In labs 01-08, this WAS the tokenizer. Now it's the baseline we'll beat.

46.text: Reverse mapping for decoding back to text.

47.text: BOS (beginning/end of sequence) gets the next available id, just past the last character.

48.text: 27 tokens total: 26 lowercase letters plus one special BOS token. This tiny vocabulary is the starting point for both tokenizers.

50.text: Print a section header. The character tokenizer is the baseline that BPE will be measured against.

53.text: Show the vocabulary breakdown: how many real characters vs control tokens.

56.text: Encode a name to character tokens: wrap with BOS on both ends, look up each character's integer ID. This is the baseline that BPE will improve upon.

57.text: Docstring for the character encoder function.

58.text: BOS + character ids + BOS. Identical to how labs 01-08 encode, just factored into a reusable function.

61.text: Reverse the encoding: map each token ID back to its character, skipping the BOS markers.

62.text: Docstring for the character decoder function.

63.text: Skip BOS tokens, map ids back to characters, join into a string.

69.text: BPE starts from the character vocabulary and folds the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token, over and over. That counting-and-merging loop really is the one GPT-2 and LLaMA use — but only the loop: they merge bytes rather than characters, run a pre-tokenization regex first so merges cannot cross word boundaries, and learn 50K-100K merges instead of the 200 here.

74.text: The fundamental tradeoff: larger vocab means shorter sequences (faster) but more embedding parameters.

78.text: Print a section header for the BPE tokenizer training phase.

82.text: 200 merges is tiny next to GPT-2's 50,000, and still enough to take this corpus from one token per character to 1.84 characters per token. The knob trades embedding rows for sequence length, and every number further down this file moves when you change it.

84.text: Everything starts at the character level, so the very first pair count is over single letters. Each merge then reshapes the corpus the next merge will count, which is why the vocabulary is order-dependent.

85.text: This corpus starts at the character level. Each sequence is still just BOS, characters, and BOS before any merges are learned.

87.text: Reuse the same BOS id so char and BPE tokenizers are comparable.

88.text: 27 base tokens before any merges happen.

90.text: Now turn each name into a list of token ids so the merge loop can operate on integer sequences rather than raw strings.

91.text: Comment: build the initial corpus by wrapping each name with BOS and converting to integer IDs.

92.text: The corpus starts as character-level token sequences, identical to what the char tokenizer produces.

93.text: Build the initial corpus for BPE training: each name becomes a list of integer token IDs, starting at character granularity.

94.text: Wrap with BOS, convert characters to integer ids. This is the starting point BPE will compress.

95.text: Accumulate each tokenized name into the corpus list. This gives us the complete training set that BPE will iteratively compress through merges.

98.text: Once the corpus is integerized, the next step is counting adjacent pairs. That pair-frequency table drives the whole tokenizer.

110.text: Simple dictionary to accumulate pair frequencies.

111.text: Scan every tokenized name in the corpus.

112.text: Slide a window of size 2 across each sequence.

113.text: The guard that makes the whole tokenizer work, and the easiest line in the lab to leave out. BPE_BOS is the most frequent token in the corpus — two per name — so without this skip the greedy loop spends its best merges gluing the delimiter onto letters ('n'+'<BOS>', '<BOS>'+'a'), the standalone end-of-name token stops surviving encoding, and generation runs forever. Note it skips the pair, not the position, so letter pairs either side of a BOS are still counted.

115.text: Each pair is a tuple of two adjacent token ids.

116.text: Increment the count. The pair with the highest count will be merged next.

117.text: Return the complete frequency dictionary. The pair with the highest count will be merged next.

120.text: The core merge operation: scan every sequence left-to-right, replacing adjacent tokens matching the pair with the new merged ID. This is greedy — the leftmost match wins.

121.text: Docstring for merge_pair: replace every occurrence of a given pair with a new single token ID.

122.text: Allocate a fresh corpus list that will hold the post-merge versions of every sequence. We rebuild rather than mutate in place to keep the logic clean.

124.text: Walk through the old sequence building a new one token by token, replacing any occurrence of the target pair with the merged token along the way.

125.text: Manual index, we sometimes skip ahead by 2 when we find the pair.

126.text: Walk through the sequence looking for the target pair.

127.text: Pattern matching: if the current token and the next match our target pair, emit the merged token and skip ahead by two positions.

128.text: Replace the pair with the single merged token, this is where compression happens.

129.text: Skip past both original tokens since we consumed them as one.

130.text: Else branch: no pair match at this position. Fall through to copy the current token unchanged.

131.text: No match here, keep the original token.

132.text: Move the scan pointer forward by one position. We only skip by two when we find and merge the target pair; otherwise we advance normally.

133.text: This name is done, add its merged sequence to the new corpus.

134.text: Return the fully merged corpus. Every sequence is now shorter by the number of merges that fired.

137.text: Step 2 comment: iteratively merge the most frequent pair. Each merge creates a new token and shrinks all sequences.

139.text: The merge table records what was merged — it IS the tokenizer, replayed during encoding.

140.text: The merge table: maps each learned pair to its new token id. This IS the tokenizer.

141.text: Tracks the growing vocabulary size as merges create new tokens.

148.text: The text each token id stands for, built up as merges are learned rather than reconstructed on demand. Searching the merge table on every decode would cost O(vocab) per token, which at 200 merges over 32K names is the difference between this file finishing in seconds and finishing in minutes.

149.text: BOS maps to the empty string: it is a control token marking where a name starts and ends, not a character anyone types. Decoding therefore drops it for free, with no special case in bpe_decode.

152.text: Decode one token id by recursively unpacking merge history until it reaches base characters.

153.text: Docstring: decode a single BPE token ID to its string representation, recursively expanding merges.

154.text: Decoding a token is now a single dict lookup. The recursive walk down the merge history happened once, at training time, when token_text was filled in.

157.text: Human-friendly token display for the training log.

158.text: Docstring: like bpe_decode_token but keeps BOS visible as '|' for human-readable output.

159.text: The training log needs BOS to stay visible, so display keeps it as | while real decoding drops it. Same table, two readings — useful when you want to see where the delimiters landed.

162.text: Helper function for the training log: convert any token ID to a human-readable string.

164.text: The merge table prints token ids as text, and a bare <BOS> tag is clearer there than a pipe. Worth having both spellings, because the whole point of the guard above is that BOS should never appear inside a merged token.

167.text: Announce the training loop. From here on, each iteration finds the most frequent pair and folds it into a new token.

168.text: Announce how many merge operations we will perform.

169.text: Header row for the training log: the merge index, the pair of token ids being merged, a readable rendering of that pair, how often it occurred, and the vocabulary size after the merge.

170.text: Print dashes to separate the table header from the data rows.

172.text: Run the greedy merge loop. Earlier merges change the corpus seen by later merges, so the learned vocabulary is order-dependent.

173.text: Count all adjacent pairs in the current (possibly already-merged) corpus.

174.text: Safety check: if no pairs remain (all sequences are length 0 or 1), stop early.

178.text: Greedy selection: always merge the globally most frequent pair. Not optimal, but close — and fast.

179.text: Record the frequency of the best pair for the training log.

180.text: Assign a new token ID: simply the current vocabulary size, so IDs increment from 27 upward.

181.text: Record this merge in the table. The order matters: during encoding, merges are replayed in exactly this sequence.

182.text: A merged token's text is just its two components concatenated, and both were entered into the table before this merge existed. That is why the table can be filled in incrementally instead of unwound recursively later.

184.text: Log the first 20 merges and every 10th after that, plus the very last one — so the output stays readable.

185.text: Build a human-readable string showing which tokens were merged (e.g., 'a'+'n').

186.text: Print one row of the training log: merge number, pair IDs, visual form, frequency, and new vocab size.

188.text: Apply the merge to every sequence in the corpus. The corpus shrinks because two tokens become one wherever this pair appeared.

189.text: Increment the vocabulary size. Every merge adds exactly one new token.

191.text: Print the final BPE vocabulary size: base tokens plus all learned merges.

194.text: BPE decoding just expands every token id back into its character sequence and drops the BOS markers.

196.text: Decoding is a join over per-token lookups, with no special case for BOS because token_text[BPE_BOS] is the empty string. Merged tokens expand to several characters each, so the length of the result tells you nothing about the number of tokens that produced it.

199.text: BPE encoding replays the learned merges in training order, which is why the merge history has to be stored explicitly.

202.text: Encoding with learned merges: start from characters, then replay every merge in training order. This greedy left-to-right strategy is how GPT-2/3/4 encode text.

205.text: Start with character-level tokens, exactly like the character encoder. BPE encoding then compresses from here.

210.text: Apply merges in the order they were learned. Earlier merges captured the most frequent patterns, so they fire most often.

211.text: A merge can only fire if both of its components are currently in the sequence, so check membership before scanning. A six-letter name skips almost all 200 rules, and encoding the whole corpus gets several times cheaper for nothing.

212.text: Apply each merge by calling merge_pair on a single-element list, then unwrap. The sequence gets shorter with each applicable merge.

213.text: Return the final compressed token sequence. Common subwords are now single tokens.

216.text: The next section switches from tokenizer construction to evaluation: how much shorter are sequences, and what does the new vocabulary look like?

222.text: A mix of hand-picked and random names to show how BPE compression varies: short common names compress heavily, long unusual ones less so.

224.text: Add some random names from the dataset so the examples are not cherry-picked.

226.text: Deduplicate while preserving order and cap at 10 examples.

232.text: The delimiters are framing, not text. Counting them as tokens would inflate the compression figure — every name carries two of them — so they are shown as | and left out of every count below.

235.text: Loop through each example name, encoding it with both tokenizers for comparison.

236.text: BPE encoding: fewer tokens because common patterns like "an", "er" are now single tokens.

237.text: Drop the two BOS markers to get content tokens. This is the fix for the old ratio, which divided character tokens by BPE tokens and quietly counted the same two delimiters on both sides of the fraction.

238.text: Characters per token, not tokens per token: how much text one BPE token stands for. Measured against the raw string, it cannot be flattered by delimiters, and it is the number that transfers to any other tokenizer.

239.text: Build the readable rendering of each token for the table. bpe_display_token is used rather than bpe_decode_token so the two BOS delimiters stay visible as |, even though they are excluded from every count in the row.

240.text: The Chars column doubles as the character tokenizer's count: character encoding always produces one token per character plus two BOS markers, and the delimiters are excluded here, so characters and char-level content tokens are the same number. That is what makes the ratio column read as characters per BPE token.

252.text: Encode the entire corpus with the character tokenizer for bigram training.

253.text: Encode the same corpus with BPE. Both bigram models below then see identical text, one at character granularity and one at subword granularity, which is what makes the comparison downstream a statement about tokenization alone.

256.text: Sum up character tokens across the entire corpus.

260.text: Character-level content tokens equal the character count by definition, which is exactly why this is the right baseline: it makes the char-level compression figure read 1.00x and gives BPE something honest to beat.

262.text: Average character tokens per name — the baseline measurement.

263.text: Average BPE tokens per name — should be notably less than the character average.

264.text: The headline compression number for the whole corpus. Total characters over total content tokens — same numerator the reader can count by hand, same denominator the model actually consumes.

282.text: Show the components that were merged (which might themselves be merged tokens).

283.text: Print the learned merged tokens so the reader can inspect which subwords the greedy algorithm discovered.

288.text: Print the base tokens (a-z) that form the foundation of the vocabulary.

289.text: Show which token ID is assigned to the BOS marker.

293.text: Display every learned merge rule. Reading this table reveals what patterns the algorithm discovered: common bigrams first (like 'an', 'er'), then longer chunks.

294.text: Decode the merged token to show what string it represents (e.g., token 28 = 'an').

295.text: Decode the first component of the merge, replacing the pipe symbol with a readable BOS tag.

297.text: Print one row: the new token ID, its decoded string, and which two tokens were merged to create it.

301.text: A bigram model is the simplest possible language model: just a transition probability table. No neural network needed.

302.text: Comment: the bigram model is P(next_token | current_token), just a lookup table of transition counts.

317.text: The final section treats each tokenizer as a modeling choice: train a bigram model on both and compare likelihood plus samples.

318.text: Docstring: train a bigram model by counting transitions, smoothing, and normalizing.

319.text: 2D count matrix: counts[a][b] = how often token b follows token a.

320.text: Initialize a 2D count matrix of zeros: rows are current tokens, columns are next tokens.

323.text: Increment the count for this specific token-to-token transition.

325.text: Start the probability table empty and fill it one row at a time, one row per context token.

326.text: Process each row of counts to produce a row of probabilities.

327.text: Add-1 (Laplace) smoothing prevents zero probabilities for unseen pairs.

328.text: Laplace smoothing: add 1 to each count, then normalize. This ensures no probability is exactly zero.

329.text: Return the smoothed transition table, a full v_size x v_size matrix. That shape is why the BPE model is at a disadvantage on data: a 227 x 227 table estimated from the same 32K names is far sparser per cell than a 27 x 27 one.

332.text: Ancestral sampling from the bigram: pick a random next token weighted by the transition probabilities, repeat until BOS (end) or max length.

333.text: Docstring: sample a sequence from the bigram model by repeatedly drawing next tokens.

334.text: Start the generated sequence with BOS — the model will sample what typically follows the start marker.

337.text: Look up the probability distribution for the current (last) token.

338.text: Draw a uniform random number to use for sampling from the probability distribution.

339.text: The running total the sampler compares its random draw against. This loop is inverse-transform sampling written out by hand, which is all a bigram sampler needs and keeps the lab dependency-free.

340.text: Walk through tokens by probability until the cumulative sum exceeds the random threshold.

342.text: This token was selected, the cumulative probability exceeded our random draw.

345.text: Terminate when the sampler emits a standalone BOS. The len(tokens) > 1 guard is what stops this check firing on the seed token itself, which is the only thing in the list before the first draw.

347.text: Return the generated sequence once it terminates.

365.text: Bits per character is the only quality figure comparable across two tokenizations. Both models assign a probability to the same string, so total bits over total characters has matching units on top and bottom, and reads directly as bits of surprise per letter.

370.text: Log base 2 rather than natural log, because the unit needs to be bits for the per-character figure to mean anything. Accumulate over transitions in whatever tokenization the model uses — the tokenization only changes how the same total is chopped up.

371.text: Divide by characters, not tokens. That single choice is what makes a 27-token model and a 227-token model answerable to the same question, and it is why papers comparing different tokenizers report bits-per-character or bits-per-byte.

374.text: Per-token log-likelihood is computed only so the trap is visible in the output. It is the usual language-model metric and it is meaningless here: the two models are answering different questions, one about 27 letters and one about 227 chunks.

376.text: Accumulate total log-likelihood across all tokens.

377.text: The token counter that becomes the denominator of the average. That denominator is the whole problem with this metric: the same corpus contains far fewer BPE tokens than character tokens, so dividing by it asks a different question of each model.

378.text: Walk exactly the same transitions the bits-per-character pass walks. The only difference between the two functions is what they divide by at the end, and that difference is the whole reason one of them is comparable across tokenizations and the other is not.

379.text: For each adjacent pair in each sequence, look up the probability the model assigns to that transition.

380.text: Log probability, the fundamental unit of information theory. Sums are easier than products.

382.text: Return the average: total log-likelihood divided by number of tokens. This per-token measure is comparable across different vocab sizes.

387.text: Train the character bigram: count transitions in a 27x27 table, smooth, and normalize.

389.text: Evaluate the character bigram: compute average log-likelihood on the training data.

391.text: Character-level bits per character: 4.1196 on this run. This is the figure to compare against BPE's.

392.text: Perplexity 11.64 per token, where a token is a character. Lower perplexity does mean a better model — but only within one fixed tokenization, which is why this column is labelled NOT comparable in the output itself.

396.text: Train the BPE bigram: count transitions in a vocab_size x vocab_size table.

398.text: Evaluate the BPE bigram on the BPE-encoded corpus.

400.text: BPE reaches 3.7490 bits per character against character-level's 4.1196: one step of BPE history spans 1.84 characters, so a one-step model effectively looks further back, and that outweighs its much sparser transition table.

401.text: Per-token perplexity for BPE is 39.72, more than three times the character model's, from the model that just won on bits per character. A BPE token is a harder thing to predict, so this column ranks chunk size, not quality.

403.text: Decide the winner from bits per character rather than hard-coding it, so the conclusion follows the run instead of the other way round.

405.text: Print the contradiction rather than hiding it. Two metrics pointing opposite ways on the same pair of models is the clearest possible demonstration that one of them is not measuring what it appears to.

409.text: Samples from both bigrams, side by side. A bigram has one step of history either way, so do not expect either list to look good — what changed with the BOS fix is that both lists now terminate at all.

411.text: The BPE sampler draws from a 227x227 transition table estimated from the same 32K names, so it is far sparser than the character model's 27x27. Add-1 smoothing is carrying more weight here than it is for the baseline.

419.text: Both samplers stop when they emit a standalone BOS, and that only works because BOS was kept out of the merges. Absorb the end-of-name marker into letter pairs and it almost never survives encoding, so every sample runs to max_len.

420.text: Generate names from the character bigram. Quality is limited because each step only sees one character of context.

421.text: Sample a complete name from the character bigram by drawing from the 27x27 transition table.

422.text: Decode the character token IDs back to a readable string.

425.text: The BPE samples read no better than the character ones, and squinting at ten strings to declare a winner would be reading tea leaves. The honest claim is narrower and more interesting: both tokenizations now produce name-shaped strings that actually end.

426.text: Spelled out in the output itself, because the temptation to eyeball ten samples and declare a winner is strong. The measurable difference between these two tokenizations is the bits-per-character figure above, not the prettiness of this list.

428.text: Sample a complete name from the BPE bigram. Each step can jump through multi-character patterns.

429.text: Sample from the BPE bigram's larger transition table.

430.text: Decode BPE tokens back to a string — merged tokens expand to multiple characters automatically.

439.text: The punchline: BPE is the algorithm behind every modern LLM tokenizer. At GPT scale (50K-100K merges on internet text), it's essential to keep sequences manageable.

445.text: The takeaway leads with bits per character and prints the misleading perplexities next to it. Reporting only the metric that agrees with you is how the wrong conclusion survives.
